procedural_history.originating_court: West Bengal First Special Court at Alipore
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated November 20, 1953, convicting the appellant under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and under s. 161 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant unsuccessfully appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The High Court then certified the case under Art. 134(1)(c) of the Constitution as fit for appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court certified the case as fit for appeal, specifically on the ground that the sanction accorded in the case was not a valid sanction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sanction accorded for the prosecution of the appellant was a valid sanction.

facts: The sanction document (Ex. 6) stated the specific facts of the case: the appellant allegedly accepted a Rs. 100 bribe on May 12, 1952, for the speedy settlement of claim cases.
The document also explicitly stated that the sanctioning officer, Mr. Bokil, had applied his mind to the facts and was satisfied that prosecution was in the interests of justice.
In his testimony, Mr. Bokil stated that before granting sanction, he "went through all relevant papers" and was satisfied that the appellant should be prosecuted.
In cross-examination, Mr. Bokil admitted that the sanction document was prepared by the police and that he did not call for office records or investigate the truth of the allegations himself.
law: The sanctioning authority is not required to judge the truth of the allegations made against the accused.
The authority's duty is to review the material placed before them and decide if it is necessary in the ends of justice to accord sanction for prosecution.
The fact that a sanction document is drafted by the police does not automatically invalidate it, provided the sanctioning authority applies their mind to the case materials before signing.
application: The Court considered Mr. Bokil's testimony and the sanction document together.

It found that Mr. Bokil's statement that he reviewed all relevant papers before signing was credible, despite the document being drafted by the police. The Court found it "inconceivable" that a high-ranking officer would sign such a document blindly.

The Court reasoned that Mr. Bokil's admission that he did not investigate the truth of the case was not detrimental, as this was not his role. His responsibility was to determine if there was sufficient material to warrant a prosecution, which the papers placed before him provided.
The Court concluded that the sanction document itself contained all the necessary facts, and Mr. Bokil's evidence confirmed he had applied his mind to those facts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the sanction was valid. It found that the sanctioning officer had applied his mind to the relevant materials before him, which is the essential requirement for a valid sanction, even if he did not personally investigate the truth of the allegations or draft the sanction order himself. Therefore, the appellant's contention was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sanction accorded for the prosecution of the appellant was a valid sanction.
appellant_arguments: The sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil, did not apply his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case before granting the sanction.
This is evidenced by Mr. Bokil's statements in cross-examination where he admitted that the sanction document was prepared by the police and put before him.
Mr. Bokil also admitted that he did not call for any official records or investigate the truth of the case, which shows he did not independently assess the matter.
The sanction was therefore not a valid one, and the court could not take cognizance of the offence.
respondent_arguments: The sanction document (Ex. 6) is valid on its face, as it clearly states the facts of the case and confirms that the sanctioning authority had applied his mind.

The sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil, testified in his examination-in-chief that he had gone through all the relevant papers and was satisfied that prosecution was necessary in the interests of justice.
It is not the duty of the sanctioning authority to investigate the truth of the allegations; his role is to determine if the materials presented warrant a prosecution.
The papers placed before Mr. Bokil provided the necessary material for him to make a valid decision to grant sanction.

cases.case_name: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
cases.principle: The case was referred to for the legal principles concerning the essentials of a valid sanction for prosecution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A sanction for the prosecution of a public servant is valid if the sanctioning authority applies their mind to the materials and facts placed before them to decide that prosecution is necessary. The authority is not required to conduct an independent investigation to judge the truth of the allegations.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found the sanction to be valid by looking at the evidence as a whole. It held that the sanctioning authority's duty is not to investigate the truth of the allegations, but to determine if the materials presented to him provide the necessary basis to decide that a prosecution is warranted in the interests of justice. Despite admissions in cross-examination, the Court concluded that the sanction document itself and the authority's primary testimony showed he had sufficient material and had applied his mind to the matter.
legal_tests_applied: The role of a sanctioning authority is not to judge the truth of the allegations made against the accused by calling for records or conducting an independent investigation.

The sanctioning authority's duty is to assess the papers placed before him to determine if they provide the necessary material upon which to decide that it is necessary in the ends of justice to accord sanction for prosecution.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil, did not apply his mind because he did not call for official records was rejected, as the Court held: 'It was not for Mr. Bokil to judge the truth of the allegations made against the appellant by calling for the records of the connected claim cases or other records in connection with the matter from his office.'

The Court viewed the evidence holistically, giving weight to the contents of the sanction document and Mr. Bokil's examination-in-chief, rather than focusing solely on his admissions in cross-examination that the police prepared the document and he did not call for records.

The Court determined that the materials placed before the sanctioning authority were sufficient for him to make a valid decision, stating: 'The papers which were placed before him apparently gave him the necessary material upon which he decided that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction.'
why_respondent_won: The sanction document (Ex. 6) was found to be valid on its face, as it 'clearly states all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant' and 'clearly states that Mr. Bokil had applied his mind and was of the opinion that in the interests of justice the appellant should be prosecuted.'

The sanctioning authority's testimony in his examination-in-chief, where he stated, 'Before according sanction I went through all relevant papers and was satisfied that in the interest of justice, Shri I. B. Chatterjee should be prosecuted,' was accepted by the Court as evidence of a valid process.

The Court endorsed the respondent's view of the sanctioning authority's role, concluding that when the sanction document and Mr. Bokil's evidence are 'carefully scrutinized and read together- there can be little doubt that the sanction accorded was a valid sanction.'
